articles.title: Fuel sold as “green” in Europe may be linked to Amazon deforestation
articles.excerpt: A US supplier of “green fuels” to the EU has imported animal fats from cattle raised on illegally deforested Amazonian land, our investigation in partnership with Unearthed and Repórter Brasil shows. Diamond Green Diesel (DGD), which describes itself as the world’s second-largest renewable diesel producer, shipped at least 25 fuel deliveries worth €1.24 billion to Belgium and the Netherlands between 2025 and 20 April 2026. The fuel is made partly from beef tallow – a fat extracted during slaughter – sourced from a Brazilian supplier linked to a slaughterhouse operator facing 31 lawsuits over illegal deforestation in the Jaci-Paraná extractive reserve, in the Brazilian state of Rondônia. “Sustainable” fuel Biofuels have become a cornerstone of Europe’s plan to clean up its transport sector. articles.title: Out of sight, out of mind?
articles.excerpt: Amsterdam's streets are changing: since 1 May, billboards for flights, cars, or steaks are banned – though this won't be enforced until 2027 to give the targeted industries time to adapt. 50 cities around the world – mostly European – have similar bans in place. In 2022, France became the first European country to restrict fossil fuel ads nationwide, prohibiting ads for petrol products, coal mining energy, and hydrogen-containing carbons like fuels and plastics. Several cities in the UK and Italy have similar bans, from Florence's ban on ads for flights, cruises, fossil energy contracts, and cars, to Portsmouth, where ads for fossil fuels, single-use plastics, and junk food are banned. Spain may be next, as the government recently voted in favour of a draft bill against advertising of fossil fuels, short flights, and fossil fuel-powered vehicles. articles.title: Airplane trails trap heat, but we can easily halve them
articles.excerpt: When you watch planes in the sky, more often than not you’ll see white trails form behind them. They start as thin lines, then spread into larger artificial clouds that trap heat. These so-called contrails form when the hot, moist exhaust from a plane's engines meets the cold air of the upper atmosphere. The water vapour instantly freezes into tiny ice crystals, and that's the white line you see. Contrails warm the planet the same way CO₂ does: they absorb heat radiating off the Earth and reflect it back down. The key difference is longevity. While CO₂ lingers in the atmosphere for centuries, contrails disappear within hours. Planes fly every single day, constantly producing new ones. In 2019, the accumulated warming from all those short-lived contrails added up to roughly the same warming as all the lingering CO₂ from aviation emitted since 1940.
